klippy::klippy(position = c('top', 'right'))

We collect multiple variables for a particular purpose, knowing that social complexity can hardly be directly explained with bivariate or univariate approaches. As it is difficult to visualize information with high dimensional data; you should consider summarising all these variable into a simpler form.

Let me start from the simplest.

_____



# Introduction

This time, I will use the [data about city safety](https://safecities.economist.com/):

```{r, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE}
# clean memory
rm(list = ls()) 

# location of the data
link="https://github.com/DACSS-Visual/tabular_multivar/raw/main/data/safeCities_ecoUI.xlsx"

# 'rio' can be used to import EXCEL files:
library(rio)
safeALL=import(link)
```


These several variables are telling us information about the safety levels of some cities in the world, and are related to **D**_igital_, **H**_ealth_, **I**_nfrastructure_, **P**_ersonal_, and **E**nvironmental dimensions. For each of these dimensions, there are measures of actions taken (**In**), and results obtained (**Out**). We have 61 indicators and the overall score for 60 cities.

Let's get rid the last column (overall score):

```{r}
drop=c("Overall_Score")
keep=setdiff(names(safeALL),drop)
safe = safeALL[,keep]
```

<a id='part1'></a>

# The heatmap for a comprehensive approach

Would making a plot of 61 variables  be a good idea? A **heatmap** is the usual answer.

Making a **heatmap** in _ggplot2_ requires a file in a particular _shape_, known as the **long format**.

The data frame _safe_ is in **wide format**, that is, one observation per row (the most usual format):

```{r, eval=TRUE}
str(safe,nchar.max = 60,strict.width='cut')
```

This is how we produce a **long format**:

```{r, eval=TRUE}
library(reshape2)

safeL=melt(safe, # all the data
           id.vars = 'city') # unique id per row
head(safeL)

```


Now, the _heatmap_ using this format:

```{r, eval=TRUE}
library(ggplot2)

base = ggplot(data = safeL, 
              aes(x = variable,
                  y =city)) 

heat1= base +  geom_tile(aes(fill = value)) 
heat1
```

Heatmap could be more informative if we reorder the axes. Let's  reorder rows (cities) and rows (indicators) by the median:

```{r, eval=TRUE}
base= ggplot(data = safeL)
vars_heat=base + aes(x = reorder(variable, value, FUN=median),
                               y =reorder(city,value, FUN=median))
geoms_heat= vars_heat + geom_tile(aes(fill = value)) 

geoms_heat
```

Here you can see what rows have higher or lower colors on what set of variables. You can customize color with a gradient:

```{r, eval=TRUE}
#inverse color -1
geoms_heat = geoms_heat +
                scale_fill_gradient(low = "white",
                                    high = 'black'
                                    )
geoms_heat
```

The column names need some work:

```{r, eval=TRUE, fig.height=10}
geoms_heat + 
  labs(x="", y="") + 
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 60, 
                                         hjust = 1,
                                         size = 8),
                      axis.text.y = element_text(
                                         size = 8)) 
                
```

For sure, it would be a good idea to rename the column names. Notice the heatplot is a good idea to detect, in this case, particular city clusters, to know if what cities are doing very good, or very bad.

Would some data wrangling help the previous plot?

```{r}
safeL$type=ifelse(grepl("_In_",safeL$variable),'input','output')

safeL$variable=sub("_In_|_Out_",'_',safeL$variable)

# now we have:
head(safeL)

```
Let's use this:

```{r}
base= ggplot(data = safeL)
vars_heat=base + aes(y = reorder(variable, value, FUN=median),
                               x =reorder(city, value, FUN=median))
geoms_heat= vars_heat + geom_tile(aes(fill = value)) 

geoms_heat_fct=geoms_heat + facet_wrap(~type, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1)
geoms_heat_fct 
```
```{r, fig.height=8}
geoms_heat_fct + 
  labs(x="", y="") + 
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 60, 
                                         hjust = 1,
                                         size = 6),
                      axis.text.y = element_text(
                                         size = 8))  +
      scale_fill_gradient(low = "white",
                          high = 'black')
```

more wrangling?

```{r}

safeL$dimension=substr(safeL$variable, 1, 1)
safeL$variable=gsub("^[A-Z]_", "", safeL$variable)

#then
safeL|>head()
```
Now take a look:
```{r}
base= ggplot(data = safeL)
vars_heat=base + aes(y = variable,
                     x =reorder(city, value, FUN=median))
geoms_heat= vars_heat + geom_tile(aes(fill = value)) 

geoms_heat_fct=geoms_heat + facet_grid(dimension~type, scales = "free_y")
geoms_heat_fct + labs(x="", y="")

```

This is not working well!

Unless the city and variable names are clearly seen, this may not be a good alternative. It may when we have fewer cities and variables, which comes next.

<a id='part2'></a>

# Averaging

This is still hard to read. An alternative could be to average by dimension: 

```{r}
# Average by city and dimension
safe_avg = aggregate(value ~ city + type + dimension, 
                            data = safeL, 
                            FUN = mean, 
                            na.rm = TRUE)

# Check the result
head(safe_avg)
```

We may turn dimension into a factor to rename the levels easily. 


```{r}
newLevels=c('DIGI','ENVIR','HEALTH','INFRA','PERS')
safe_avg$dimension=factor(safe_avg$dimension,
                          levels = c("D","E","H","I","P"),
                          labels = newLevels,ordered = F)
```


Let's redo our heat map for the 'input' type:
```{r, eval=TRUE, fig.height=8}
base_ave_in= ggplot(data = safe_avg[safe_avg$type=='input',])

vars_ave_in=base_ave_in + aes(x = reorder(dimension,
                                          value,median),
                              y =reorder(city,
                                         value,
                                         median))

geoms_ave_in=vars_ave_in + geom_tile(aes(fill = value))

geoms_ave_in + 
       scale_fill_gradient(low = 'white',
                           high = "black") +
       theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90,
                                        hjust = 1,
                                        size = 8),
             axis.text.y = element_text(size = 6))
```


With the current long format, making a faceted heatplot may work better as last time:

```{r, fig.height=8}
base_ave= ggplot(data = safe_avg)

vars_ave=base_ave + aes(x = reorder(dimension,
                                          value,FUN=median),
                              y =reorder(city,
                                         value,
                                         FUN=median)) +
  facet_grid(~type,scales='free_x')

geoms_ave=vars_ave + geom_tile(aes(fill = value))

geoms_ave + 
       scale_fill_gradient(low = 'white',
                           high = "black") 
```


It did not!

We should compute a different plot for each _type_:

```{r}
# different data frames
safe_avg_out=safe_avg[safe_avg$type=='output',]
safe_avg_in=safe_avg[safe_avg$type=='input',]
```

Then, we use each type:
```{r, eval=TRUE, fig.height=8}
base_ave_out= ggplot(data = safe_avg_out)

vars_ave_out=base_ave_out + aes(x = reorder(dimension,
                                          value,median),
                              y =reorder(city,
                                         value,
                                         median))

geoms_ave_out=vars_ave_out + geom_tile(aes(fill = value))

geoms_ave_out + 
       scale_fill_gradient(low = 'white',
                           high = "black") +
       theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90,
                                        hjust = 1,
                                        size = 8),
             axis.text.y = element_text(size = 6)) + labs(x="",y='')
```

As you see, the cities have different locations according to type, which could not be captured when using facets.


## The Radar

When you have this limited amount of variables, the radar plot is an alternative:


```{r, fig.width=15, fig.height=12, eval=TRUE}
library(ggforce)

base_rd  = ggplot(safe_avg_in) + theme_light()

vars_rd= base_rd + aes(x = dimension, 
                   y = value)
geoms_rd=vars_rd + geom_shape(aes(group = city),fill = 'grey70') + coord_polar()


radar1_re = geoms_rd + facet_wrap(~reorder(city,-value, median),ncol = 10)

radar1_re
```


You could add extra customization. Let me change some defaults that help you later make improvements:

```{r, fig.width=15, fig.height=12, eval=TRUE}

radar1_re + 
            theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 8, color='black'),
                  strip.text = element_text(size = 14),
                  panel.background=element_rect(fill = "white",
                         colour = "red",
                         linewidth = 1.5,
                         linetype = "dashed"),
                  panel.grid.major=element_line(linewidth = 0.5,
                      linetype = 'solid',
                      colour = "grey")
                  ) + labs(x='', y='')
                        
```

The colors above **are not** the best choice, I just used them for you to notice where to make changes. Keep in mind that **areas are difficult to compare**, so the plots above might be used with care.


## Simplifying the Radar


The idea behind the radar plot can be represented by simpler plots:

```{r}
vars_lolli=base_rd + aes(x=reorder(city, value,median),
                         y=value)
geoms_lolli=vars_lolli+ geom_point(shape=5)+ geom_segment(aes(x=city,
                                                  y=0,
                                                  yend = value,
                                                  xend = city),
                                              color='grey',linewidth=0.2) 
geoms_lolli+ facet_grid(type~dimension) + coord_flip() + 
    theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 5)) + labs(x='', y='')
```


>Averaging treats all variables equally, but what if some indicators are more informative than others? Dimensionality reduction techniques like EFA and MDS weight variables by their contribution to underlying patterns, potentially revealing structures that simple averaging obscures

# Dimensionality Reduction

Plotting multivariate cases when three variables are present can be easily solved with facets, or adding an extra channel (i.e. _color_) to a bivariate plot. The cases above were very extreme, and they have served to reflect on the need to simplify that complexity.

We use the concept *dimensionality reduction* for these cases. The approach is similar to _averaging_ in that it will summarize the variables into a much smaller set of variables; but differs drastically from _averaging_ as the techniques will keep the relevant variables and may discard the variables not contributing to summary.

The techniques themselves are beyond this course; nevertheless, I will show you how they can be used and combined for our purposes.


Let's work  with all the **IN**put indicators:

```{r, eval=TRUE}
allIN=safe[,c(grep("_In_", names(safe) ))]
names(allIN)
```

Preserve the city names at the index:

```{r, eval=TRUE}
rownames(allIN)=safe$city

##
head(allIN)
```

With this data frame we will use the next techniques.

## Plotting with Factor Analysis (EFA)

When we averaged by dimension as we did before for the _radar plot_, we assumed all the indicators weight the same. We can use Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA) to uncover the weight of the dimensions, but also to validate what dimensions exist, and what variables really bring information in the study.

### Previous steps...

EFA uses the correlation matrix (CM) as input. Once we have it, we can compute the KMO to assess the suitability if the variables to the multivariate process:

```{r}
#### notice you may need to install 'polycor' and 'psych'
## compute CM 
CM=polycor::hetcor(allIN)$correlations # 'hetcor' in case you have numerical and categorical

##CM is suitable
KMO_tested=psych::KMO(CM) 
##KMO measures how much the variables share common variance
##low values mean a variable is mostly noise
KMO_tested$MSA
```

The value above 0.6 seems acceptable, but we still  should drop the  variables that individually bring noise to the analysis:
```{r}
# only the variables with a proper MSAi will remain
keep_vars = KMO_tested$MSAi >= 0.5
allIN_kmo_ok = allIN[, keep_vars]
ncol(allIN_kmo_ok)
```

With this number of variables, we can determine the appropriate number of dimensions:
```{r}
## Detect the dimensions
CM_kmo_ok=polycor::hetcor(allIN_kmo_ok)$correlations
psych::fa.parallel(CM_kmo_ok, fm = "pa", fa = "fa",plot = F,n.obs = nrow(allIN_kmo_ok))
```

We know that the set of var **THREE** dimension will get the best of the remaining informative variables, so we compute the EFA:

```{r}
#4. Compute the new dimensions
res_fa = psych::fa(CM_kmo_ok, n.obs = nrow(allIN_kmo_ok),
                    nfactors = 3, rotate = "varimax", fm = "pa")
```

From the **res_fa** object we can first determine how  dimensions may be named, for that you read the **factor loadings**:
```{r}
print(res_fa$loadings)
```

Each of the three summarizing factors have a higher or lower affinity to a particular variable (based on the values seen above). We can arguably propose this:

## Factor Summary Table

| Factor | Proposed Name | Key Indicators (Loadings ≥ 0.50) | Conceptual Definition |
|--------|--------------|----------------------------------|----------------------|
| **PA1** | Foundational Public Services & Social Governance | • Access to Safe & Quality Food (0.781)<br>• Expenditure on Social Security (0.711)<br>• Capacity of Judicial System (0.690)<br>• Water Infrastructure (0.645)<br>• Universal Healthcare Coverage (0.637)<br>• Pedestrian Friendliness (0.597)<br>• Privacy Policy (0.575) | Baseline institutional capacity to deliver essential welfare services, basic infrastructure, and core governance functions that support everyday quality of life. |
| **PA2** | Healthcare System Performance | • Quality of Health Services (0.915)<br>• Access to Healthcare (0.769)<br>• Health Infrastructure (0.617) | Effectiveness and accessibility of clinical care delivery, reflecting the operational performance of the health system distinct from policy commitments. |
| **PA3** | Crisis Preparedness & Environmental Resilience | • Waste Management (0.701)<br>• Pandemic Preparedness (0.692)<br>• Hazard Monitoring (0.605)<br>• Disaster Management & Business Continuity (0.586)<br>• Cybersecurity Preparedness (0.548) | Forward-looking systemic capacities to anticipate, absorb, and recover from acute shocks and chronic stresses across environmental, health, and digital domains. |


Given we have 'names' for the factors, we can pay attention to the value values of the variables for each city. For that, we retrieve the scores:

```{r}
city_scores = psych::factor.scores(allIN_kmo_ok, res_fa)$scores|>as.data.frame()
head(city_scores)
```

These scores are standardized values that we can normalize (0-100) for easier reading of the plots:
```{r, message=FALSE}
# normalizing
library(BBmisc)
efa_scores_norm=normalize(city_scores, 
                       method = "range", 
                       margin=2, # by column
                       range = c(0, 100))

# new  vars

city_scores$governance=efa_scores_norm[,1]
city_scores$health_system=efa_scores_norm[,2]
city_scores$preparedness=efa_scores_norm[,3]

city_scores[,4:6]
```

After so much stats, we can produce a simple plot like a lollipop. Let's turn those columns into a long shape, and plot:

```{r, fig.height=8}

##reshaping
city_scores_wide=city_scores[,4:6]
city_scores_wide$city=rownames(city_scores_wide)
city_scores_long=melt(city_scores_wide,id.vars = 'city')

##plotting
baseefa=ggplot(data=city_scores_long) + theme_classic() 

varsefa=baseefa + aes(x=reorder(city, value,median),y=value)

geomsefa= varsefa + geom_point(shape=5, aes(color=value>75))+
                    geom_segment(aes(x=city,y=0,yend = value,xend = city),
                                 color='grey70',linewidth=0.2)
geomsefa +  facet_grid(~variable) + coord_flip() +
            theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10)) +
            labs(title = "Safety of Cities",
                 subtitle = "A 3-dimensional approach",
                 x="", y='Scores', color="Above 75 points")
```

Of course, you may use a scatter plot:

```{r}
base_efa_cor=ggplot(city_scores) + theme_light()
vars_efa_cor=base_efa_cor + aes(x=governance, y=health_system, color=preparedness)
geoms_efa_cor = vars_efa_cor + geom_point(size=4)
geoms_efa_cor + scale_color_viridis_c(direction = -1,option = 'cividis')
```

Alternatively,
```{r}
# city names back to data
city_scores$namecity=row.names(city_scores)

library(ggrepel)

base_efa_cor=ggplot(city_scores) + theme_light()
vars_efa_cor=base_efa_cor + aes(x=governance, y=health_system)
geoms_efa_cor = vars_efa_cor + geom_text_repel(aes(color=preparedness, label=namecity),
                                               max.overlaps = 20)
geoms_efa_cor + scale_color_viridis_c(direction = -1,option = 'cividis')

```




## Plotting with MDS 


You can use multidimensional scaling (MDS) to synthesize  **all the variables in a two dimensional plot**. This will create a **map** that will allow you to visualize "neighborhoods of similarity"  of the cases (cities). 


MDS requires as input the **distance matrix** among cases, notice we will use the **city_scores_wide** data frame, which was built without the non-informative variables:

```{r, eval=TRUE}
library(cluster)
dist_in_safe=cluster::daisy(city_scores_wide[,c('governance','health_system','preparedness')],
                            metric = 'gower') # 'gower' in case you have numerical and categorical
```

> Notice we ran MDS on the 3 EFA dimensions (not 61 variables) to visualize how cities relate in the reduced factor space

Using the distances, we can try MDS and check the goodness of fit:
```{r, eval=TRUE}
theMap=cmdscale(dist_in_safe,k = 2,eig = T)
theMap$GOF[2]
```

We are recovering around 62% of the information (thus losing the around 38%). While not terrible, we should try a **non-metric MDS** approach, which often fits complex social data better:

```{r}
theMap$GOF
```

We can try an alternative technique:
```{r}
# you may need to install 'MASS' library
theMap_iso=MASS::isoMDS(dist_in_safe,k = 2)
theMap_iso$stress
```

The stress value of ~0.15 indicates an acceptable fit — better than the classical MDS result, though ideally stress should be below 0.10 for a reliable 2D representation.

### Stress Interpretation (Non-metric MDS)

| Stress Value | Quality | Interpretation |
|--------------|---------|----------------|
| < 0.05 | Excellent | Perfect representation |
| < 0.10 | Good | Reliable 2D map |
| < 0.20 | Acceptable | Suitable for exploration |
| > 0.20 | Poor | Consider more dimensions |

**Our result:** ~0.15 → **Acceptable for exploratory visualization** ✓


Let's use this last result
```{r, echo=FALSE, eval=FALSE}
library(MASS)
# Note the Capital S
sh = Shepard(dist_in_safe, theMap_iso$points)

plot(sh, pch = 20, xlab = "Dissimilarity", ylab = "Distance", main = "Shepard Plot")
lines(sh$x, sh$yf, type = "S")
```
```{r}
city_scores_wide$dim1=theMap_iso$points[,1]
city_scores_wide$dim2=theMap_iso$points[,2]
```

Using those values, see the map:

```{r, fig.height=8}

city_scores_wide$city=row.names(city_scores_wide)
base_mds=ggplot(city_scores_wide) + theme_light()
vars_mds=base_mds + aes(x=dim1,y=dim2,label=city)
geoms_mds=vars_mds + geom_text_repel(size=4,min.segment.length = 0) 

# 
geoms_mds
```

## Plotting with Cluster info

**Clustering** comes in handy to improve the previous viz. Each city will be grouped by affinity (similarity). That grouping depends on the technique used.

Let's compare the hierarchical clustering technique (HC), a technique that clusters every row (city).

### Using HC  

HC requires you know how many clusters to detect. That analysis is beyond the session (and course). Let's just _assume_ we need 5 clusters:

```{r, message=FALSE}
library(factoextra)

res.hc= hcut(dist_in_safe, k = 5)

## Add them to data frame
city_scores_wide$hc=as.factor(res.hc$cluster)
```

Let's redo the previous plot:

```{r, eval=TRUE}
base_mds_hc=ggplot(city_scores_wide) + theme_light()
vars_mds_hc=base_mds_hc + aes(x=dim1,y=dim2,label=city, color=hc)
geoms_mds_hc=vars_mds_hc + geom_text_repel(size=4,max.overlaps = 20, min.segment.length = 0) 

# 
geoms_mds_hc

```

Notice that the ideal viz will separate clearly the country groups, but that is not happening. In fact, it may be due to the nature of the HC technique, which will not inform about outliers; that being said, there are other clustering techniques (namely dbscan) that do show cases (countries) that do not belong to any cluster. Several other reason are explored in other courses.


# Method Comparison

| Method | Best For | Limitations |
|--------|----------|-------------|
| **Comprehensive Heatmap** | Showing all data, detecting outliers | Overwhelming with >50 variables |
| **Averaging** | Simple summaries, policy dashboards | Assumes equal weights, loses detail |
| **EFA** | Uncovering latent structures, weighting variables | Requires statistical assumptions |
| **MDS** | Visualizing similarity/dissimilarity | Loses information (check GOF/stress) |
| **Clustering** | Grouping similar cases | Sensitive to distance metric, k choice |
